annotations.text: We interpret this as solitary accountability: responsibility that is not only heavy but also carried alone, with no one to check a judgement against.
We interpret this as working against the body clock: a bodily cost that nurses manage privately and rarely raise at work.
We interpret this as invisibility to the day team, a gap in the organisation’s view of its own night work.
After midnight it’s me and one healthcare assistant for thirty-two patients. If something goes wrong, there’s no one to ask.
You make the call, and you carry it home with you.
Around four in the morning my brain just stops. You check the chart three times and still don’t trust it.
Days see the tidy ward in the morning. They never see how it got that way.
Nobody from management has ever come on at night.
We interpret this as fatigue as the price of the job: tiredness is accepted as normal, so it is not treated as a problem for the organisation to solve.
annotations.note: Fatigue as the price of the job

annotations.text: We interpret this as owed recovery: the rest that nurses are due, but which is absorbed by the rest of life.
We interpret this as a life out of step: night work separates nurses from the rhythm of daily life at home.
Everyone is tired. If you say it out loud it sounds like you are not suited to the job.
After a night shift I tell myself I will sleep all day, but then the laundry, then the shopping, and it is evening.
My children are going to school when I get home. We pass each other at the door.
We interpret this as autonomy in the quiet hours: what staff may experience as being alone, managers read as being trusted.

clusterComments.cl_1794738095030_gb5j: Same night conditions, read differently: managers (not staff) call it trust and autonomy. Both hospitals had a night coordinator on every floor, so nights may feel safer from the manager’s seat.

annotations.text: We interpret this as support at a distance: help that exists on paper but arrives late or in the form of a phone call.
We interpret this as fatigue as an individual matter: the organisation provides the roster, and the nurse is expected to cope with the rest.

clusterComments.cl_1794738098047_iq81: The manager’s version of the same idea: the roster is fair, the tiredness is yours.

annotations.text: At night they run their own ship. I trust them to.
I’m on the phone from home if they need me, but I can’t be on the ward.
I can roster fairly, but I can’t roster away tiredness. That’s on them to manage.
We interpret this as escalation without back-up: a duty to act that is not matched by someone to act with.

clusterComments.cl_1794738095030_gb5j: Managers confirm what staff describe: a duty to act with nobody to act with.

annotations.text: We interpret this as rostering as a hidden inequity: the burden of night work falls most on the people with the least say.
We interpret this as nights outside our line of sight: the organisation cannot fix what it does not see.
annotations.note: Nights outside our line of sight

annotations.text: We say ‘just escalate’, but escalate to whom? There is nobody.
Nights go to whoever can’t say no. Usually the new grads and the casuals.
I find out about a bad night from the incident report on Monday.
Nurses spoke about exhaustion as something that simply comes with nursing. Complaining was seen as weak, and the word gaman (enduring quietly) came up in all three groups.

annotations.text: The best nurses I have grow on nights. Nobody is looking over their shoulder.

clusters.translationSummary: Hartwell’s “solitary accountability” and Reyes’s “escalation without back-up” describe the same thing from two sides: a nurse who must decide alone. Nguyen’s “autonomy in the quiet hours” describes the same conditions but reads them as trust, so it is translated refutationally.
clusters.synthesisNote: At night, responsibility is carried by one person with little back-up. Whether this is felt as isolation or as autonomy depends on who is speaking: staff nurses report isolation, managers report trust.
clusters.cerqualExplanation: Moderate confidence: the finding is well supported, but one manager-focused study reads the same conditions differently.
clusters.cerqualLimNote: Minor concerns in two of the three studies (limited reflexivity).
clusters.cerqualCohNote: One study (Nguyen) reads the same conditions as autonomy, so the finding is not fully consistent.
clusters.cerqualAdeqNote: Three studies, each with rich quotes.
clusters.cerqualRelNote: Hospital wards in four countries; relevant to the review question.

clusters.thirdOrderTitle: Fatigue is normalised and left to the individual
clusters.translationSummary: Hartwell’s “working against the body clock” matches Sato’s “fatigue as the price of the job”: tiredness is expected and managed privately. Sato’s “owed recovery” and “a life out of step” extend this into days off and home life. Nguyen’s “fatigue as an individual matter” shows managers holding the same view.
clusters.synthesisNote: Staff nurses and managers both treat the costs of night work as normal and as the individual’s to manage, so fatigue is rarely raised as an organisational problem.
clusters.cerqualExplanation: High confidence: consistent across all four studies and both subgroups.

clusters.thirdOrderTitle: Night work sits outside the organisation’s view
clusters.translationSummary: Hartwell’s “invisibility to the day team” corresponds to Reyes’s “nights outside our line of sight”: nurses and managers both say nights are not seen. Nguyen’s “support at a distance” and Reyes’s “rostering as a hidden inequity” show what follows when no one is looking.
clusters.synthesisNote: The organisation cannot see night work, so support arrives late and the burden falls on those with the least say.
clusters.cerqualExplanation: Moderate confidence: consistent, but parts of the finding rest on a single study.
clusters.cerqualAdeqNote: Fewer quotes for the rostering idea (one study only).

loa.title: Night work as an unseen, individually carried burden
loa.flow: [Night work is out of view] ➔ [Responsibility without back-up] + [Fatigue left to the individual] ➔ [Nurses endure alone]
loa.narrative: Night work sits outside the organisation’s view. Because it is not seen, nurses carry responsibility with little back-up and manage their own fatigue. Staff describe this as isolation, while managers describe it as trust: the same conditions, two readings.
loa.relateProcess: Studies were compared by their main concepts and by who was speaking (staff nurses or managers) and where.
loa.relateOutcome: Staff and manager studies agree on fatigue and on nights being unseen. They differ on whether working alone is isolation or autonomy.
loa.reviewQuestion: How do nurses and nurse managers experience night shifts in hospitals, and how do their accounts differ?
loa.translationDefinitions: Reciprocal: concepts that describe the same idea in different words. Refutational: concepts that describe the same conditions but disagree about what they mean.
loa.translationProcess: Reviewer A translated study by study, starting from Hartwell (index paper: richest account). Reviewer B’s extraction was compared and merged before translation.
loa.alternativeInterpretations: We considered whether the “autonomy” reading reflects role (manager) or setting (night coordinator on every floor). The papers cannot separate the two.
loa.modelContext: Applies to hospital wards with small night teams. It may not apply where a senior nurse is always on the ward.
